title: Zhong invested in Unitree but missed the follow-on: patient capital can also get stuck by fund cycles
dek: Vertex was the sole institutional investor in Unitree's Pre-A+ round in 2020, but in the 2023 round it couldn't follow on because its own USD fund was expiring and it was raising a new fund. Doubling down tests not just vision, but the rhythm match between fund and project.
why: A person who has done hard-tech VC for 17 years within Singapore's sovereign capital system lays out the betting logic for chips, robotics, and low-altitude economy, and candidly reviews why he missed ByteDance and the follow-on in Unitree.
who: Suitable for founders and investors focused on hard tech, robotics, and the full cycle of USD fund raising, investing, managing, and exiting, especially those who want to know how a sovereign-backed VC makes independent judgments and how to review missing a follow-on.
skip: From 27:35 to 33:28, it covers Singapore clan associations, the Zhongyuan Festival, and Chinese cohesion, which is weakly related to investment judgment.

points.h: They started investing when chips were cheaper than potato chips
points.body: Vertex invested in semiconductors as early as 2011, and in 2012 invested in a new materials company making solid-state batteries. At the time, domestic VCs hardly looked at these because the internet was at its peak. Zheng Juncong told a joke: chips are called chips, and everyone thought a chip was cheaper than a potato chip, so no one invested, because chips relied on imports and sold for only one US dollar each. He judged that chip technology content was extremely high, from millions of lines of code to billions of lines of code, and all electronic products, from cars to the cloud, would need them. The pitch for investing in chips also changed with the times: initially it was about domestic production being tax-exempt, later it was about iterating around the mobile phone supply chain, and now it's about being bottlenecked plus next-generation applications like optical computing.

points.h: IC can pass by half, and there's a golden share
points.body: Vertex's investment committee does not require a unanimous vote; a majority is enough, and they even hold ad hoc meetings on weekends if a project needs to be submitted to IC. More uniquely, there's a golden share: a partner has one chance a year to insist on investing in a company even if the IC does not approve. Voting is secret; you don't know whether a partner voted for or against, because they don't want people to go easy on each other and give up independent judgment. The voting choice is also tied to project outcomes long-term; if a project fails but you voted for it, it will be traced back and counted in your score, and when distributing carry, it will be brought out to look at. This mechanism is designed to force independent judgment, not votes based on personal relationships.

points.h: They don't chase trends because founders of hotly contested deals get arrogant
points.body: Vertex explicitly does not invest in projects that are particularly sought after in the market. Zheng Juncong gives two reasons: first, everyone competing drives up the valuation; second, when entrepreneurs are chased, they focus on valuation, feel that investors are all flattering them, and won't settle down to build the company, so the success rate is actually lower. They value entrepreneurs who do solid technology, have patience, want to create value, and don't rely on hype. They have zero tolerance for financial fraud, because Singapore cares a lot about integrity and authenticity, and once fraud is discovered, they will definitely withdraw. This style also explains why they haven't invested in many money-burning internet companies.

points.h: If they could choose again on large models, they still wouldn't invest, because it's like the internet
points.body: Over the past four years, the undisputed hot spot for investment in China has been AI large models. Vertex did not make a move in the first three or four years, which is very unusual among first-tier funds. Zheng Juncong's reasoning: large model startups in China have no advantage; the advantage will come from customers, data, and application scenarios, and they need to be big enough and able to burn a lot of money. It's essentially like the internet playbook, and the business model is still unclear. The two biggest internal voices were "this will definitely take off, China will definitely have large models" and "the model risk is high, it may continue to burn money like the internet, and existing large internet companies have a higher probability of success." He admits this discourages young investors who want to participate, but they hold back from investing because they firmly believe hard tech is the advantage.

points.h: Singapore certification: swap chips and software, then export
points.body: Zheng Juncong believes Singapore can help Chinese entrepreneurs solve two things: product internationalization and product security. Products made with China's manufacturing, design, and innovation capabilities are wanted worldwide, but when they encounter geopolitics, politicians will obstruct them on the grounds that "Chinese products are unsafe, robots might carry things and hit people on the street." Singapore, as a neutral, transparent, and reputable country, can achieve "Citified by Singapore"—chips certified here, or swapped with chips and software from here, then exported from here, allowing products to enter other countries. He also criticizes "Singapore Washing": companies that move here just to slap on a label without actual operations and R&D—that's the term he least wants to hear.

points.h: Boston Dynamics costs over a hundred thousand USD; Wang Xingxing sells for just over ten thousand
points.body: In 2019, Zheng Juncong went to Boston for a board meeting and visited Boston Dynamics. He wanted to buy a robot dog, but they said it wasn't for sale, and the cost was about a hundred thousand USD. After returning to China, he judged that China is strong in hardware, so someone must be doing it, and had his team search all Chinese robotics teams, finding Wang Xingxing. At the time, the robot dog was already very agile, able to stand up and bow. He asked if it was controlled by AI, and Wang Xingxing said no, it used his own algorithm. When asked about cost, Wang Xingxing didn't mention cost, only said it currently sells for about ten thousand USD. The same dog, others cost over a hundred thousand, he sells for just over ten thousand. Zheng Juncong judged there was commercialization potential; cost is a very important element in technological innovation.

points.h: Missed the follow-on in Unitree: fund expired, not enough bullets
points.body: Vertex was the sole institutional investor in Unitree's Pre-A+ round in 2020, but the follow-on only came in September 2024, by which time Unitree had already produced the G1 bipedal robot and its valuation had soared. Why didn't they follow on earlier? Zheng Juncong reviews: when they invested, they saw a market of several billion, but didn't see that bipedal robots could be made; in the 2023 round, Matrix Partners and Shunwei came in, and they also wanted to invest, but their USD fund was just at the end of its term and they were raising a new fund, so they didn't have enough bullets to add to the position, and thus missed that round. He calls it a huge regret, and says this made them reflect; now the new fund requires starting to raise new capital once 65% is invested, reserving 20% to 30% for follow-on investments.

points.h: Wang Xingxing raised funds slowly, but that honed mass production consistency
points.body: Zheng Juncong believes Wang Xingxing doesn't need to be better at fundraising; the current fundraising pace is actually the best. If he had been very good at fundraising back then and raised a lot in the next round, the playbook might have been different—flashy, more money-burning, no discipline in running the company, not nitpicking cost details, and the models produced might not be profitable. After AI came, many companies want to copy Unitree, thinking the barrier isn't high, it's just algorithms, and they can catch up quickly with AI. Zheng Juncong says everyone can get algorithms to about the same level, but the real gap is mass production and consistency, which is built up from all past investment and time, and no other company in the market has his mass production consistency.

points.h: A crude way to judge a bubble: look at who is starting companies
points.body: Asked whether China's embodied intelligence has a bubble, Zheng Juncong says no, because the market is still expanding and in its creation phase. He gives a rough indicator for judging a bubble: when the entrepreneurs you attract are not real entrepreneurs, but people who were in big companies without entrepreneurial spirit, who see others succeed and raise money, and jump out saying they want to start a company too—that's the node where a bubble appears. Now he sees entrepreneurs who are "I've done this and that," very strong, capable people. He quotes Lee Kuan Yew saying the market needs a bubble, like beer without foam isn't tasty, but too much foam isn't good either; it should be controlled at an appropriate ratio.

terms.def: Vertex's investment committee mechanism: a partner can, once a year, force an investment in a project that the IC has rejected.
Distributions to Paid-In Capital: the money LPs actually get back divided by the capital invested; the hardest metric sovereign funds use to evaluate GPs.
Refers to Chinese companies that only move their headquarters to Singapore as a label, without actual operations and R&D.
Electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft: a core category in the low-altitude economy, using multiple electric rotors instead of a helicopter's single engine.
Using AI to research new materials, chemical structures, and other problems that humans cannot calculate.
